description: Types of motion, linkages, conversion mechanisms and cam profiles explained clearly.
content_html:
Four Types of Motion

Mechanical systems transmit and transform movement. Before designing a mechanism you must identify what type of motion is needed at the output. There are four types that engineers work with every day.

Rotary motion is spinning around a fixed axis — a motor shaft, a gear, a wheel. Linear motion is movement in a straight line, such as the travel of a drill bit moving into a workpiece. Reciprocating motion is back-and-forth movement along a straight line — a piston, a saw blade or a needle in an industrial sewing machine. Oscillating motion is a swinging or rocking motion around a fixed point, like a pendulum or a windscreen wiper arm.

In the examination you must use the correct technical terms — answers like “goes round and round” or “goes sideways” are not credited. A motor produces rotary motion; a piston produces reciprocating motion.

Key Fact

The four types of motion are rotary (spinning around an axis), linear (straight line), reciprocating (back-and-forth straight line) and oscillating (swinging around a fixed point). Most mechanisms convert one type of motion into another.

Linkages and Conversion of Motion

A linkage is a set of rigid bars joined by pivots that transmits or changes the direction of movement. Engineers use linkages when they need to transmit force around corners, reverse direction, or change the shape of a motion path.

The simplest linkage is a reverse linkage (bell crank). Pushing one arm down causes the other arm to push outward — the motion direction changes by 90°. Bicycle brake levers use this principle: squeezing the handle pulls a cable that pushes brake pads against the wheel rim. A parallel linkage keeps two bars moving in the same direction — used in toy train pantographs and car suspension systems.

The crank and slider mechanism is the fundamental converter of rotary motion into reciprocating motion. A rotating crank pin is connected to a slider (piston) by a connecting rod. As the crank rotates, the slider moves back and forth. Every internal combustion engine uses this principle — the rotating crankshaft drives the pistons up and down.

The reverse is also possible: a reciprocating steam engine drives a piston back and forth, which turns a crankshaft via a connecting rod to produce rotary motion at the wheels. Engineers describe this as converting reciprocating to rotary motion.

Cams and Followers

A cam is a specially shaped piece that rotates and pushes a component called a follower up and down as it turns. The key principle: the position of the follower at any instant depends entirely on the radius of the cam at the point of contact. Where the cam radius is large, the follower is pushed up. Where the radius is small, the follower drops down. This is the examiner’s most-tested cam concept — you must be able to explain it, not just name it.

Key Fact

The follower’s position at any moment is determined by the cam profile — specifically the radius of the cam at the point of contact. A large radius pushes the follower high; a small radius lets it drop. The cam profile is therefore what engineers adjust to control the follower’s movement pattern.

Four cam profiles appear in engineering exam questions:

  • Pear cam — egg-shaped profile. The follower rises slowly to a maximum height and then drops quickly. Used in car engine valve timing, where a valve must open slowly and snap shut.
  • Eccentric (circular) cam — a circular disc with the pivot offset from the centre. As it rotates the follower rises and falls smoothly in a simple harmonic pattern. Used in pumps and simple oscillating machines.
  • Snail (drop) cam — the follower rises very gradually around most of the rotation, then drops almost vertically as it reaches the “snail’s tail” drop. Used in clock escapements and stamping machines where a sudden downward force is needed.
  • Heart cam — heart-shaped profile that converts the continuous rotation into a back-and-forth motion of equal rate in both directions. Used in mechanisms where a constant-rate reciprocation is needed.

Choosing the Right Mechanism

When an engineer needs to convert motion, they select the mechanism based on the motion required and the forces involved. To convert rotary to reciprocating: use a cam or a crank and slider. To change the direction of a force: use a linkage (bell crank, reverse linkage). To transmit rotary motion between shafts that are far apart or at an angle: use gears, chains or belts (covered in Lesson 3).

At Rolls-Royce Turbine Assemblies in Derby, precision cams in the engine-control unit govern the opening and closing of fuel valves with timings accurate to thousandths of a second. The cam profile is machined to tolerances of ±0.005 mm because any deviation changes the valve timing and affects thrust output. This real-world context shows why understanding cam profiles matters beyond the classroom.
exam_tip_html: If asked to “explain how a cam produces movement in the follower”, use the phrase cam profile and link it to the radius: “As the cam rotates, the radius at the contact point changes. Where the radius is greater, the follower is pushed further up; where the radius is smaller, the follower drops down.” Simply naming the cam type without explaining the radius principle will not earn full marks. Also remember: exam questions use the technical names — write reciprocating not “back and forth” and rotary not “round and round”.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four types of motion are rotary (spinning), linear (straight line), reciprocating (back-and-forth along a line) and oscillating (swinging around a pivot) — you must use the correct technical names in exam answers.
  • Linkages use rigid bars and pivots to transmit or redirect force; the crank-and-slider mechanism converts rotary motion to reciprocating motion (and vice versa).
  • A cam profile determines the follower’s movement — the follower rises when the cam radius is large and drops when it is small; the four named profiles (pear, eccentric, snail, heart) each produce a different motion pattern.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes reciprocating motion?
A) Spinning continuously around a fixed axis
B) Moving in a straight line in one direction only
C) Moving back and forth along a straight line
D) Swinging around a fixed point
practice_questions.marks: C) Moving back and forth along a straight line [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Name the type of motion produced by each of the following:
(a) A motor shaft spinning
(b) A piston moving inside a cylinder
(c) A windscreen wiper arm
practice_questions.marks:
(a) Rotary motion [1 mark]
(b) Reciprocating motion [1 mark]
(c) Oscillating motion [1 mark]
[3 marks total]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the shape of a cam profile controls the movement of a follower.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 2 marks:
- The follower's position depends on the radius of the cam at the point of contact.
- Where the cam radius is large, the follower is pushed up; where the radius is small, the follower drops down.
- The profile (outline shape) of the cam is designed to create the desired movement pattern in the follower.
[2 marks — both marks require a link between cam profile/radius and follower position]

practice_questions.text: Describe how a crank and slider mechanism converts rotary motion into reciprocating motion. Your answer should refer to the key components involved.
practice_questions.type: 4 marks — Describe Stages of a Process
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct point, up to 4 marks:
- A crank (offset pin or arm) is attached to a rotating shaft.
- A connecting rod links the crank pin to a slider (piston or sliding block).
- As the crank rotates, the connecting rod pushes and pulls the slider.
- The slider moves back and forth in a straight line (reciprocating motion).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Westbrook Machinery Ltd manufactures food-packaging equipment. One machine uses a cam mechanism to open and close a packaging flap 60 times per minute. The flap must open slowly and close quickly to allow product to fall in without jamming.

Which cam profile would be most suitable for this application? Explain your choice.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Explain Application of a Property or Material
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5-6): Correctly identifies the pear cam profile and gives a detailed explanation linking the profile shape to the required motion: the long, gradually curving lobe allows slow opening of the flap, while the short, sharp drop on the pear’s ‘nose’ produces the quick closing action. Explains the mechanism by which the follower position is set by the cam radius, and links this to the packaging application (product falls through without jamming).

Secure (3-4): Correctly identifies pear cam. Explains that it produces a slow rise and a quick drop, linked to the requirement. May not fully explain the cam-radius mechanism.

Developing (2): Names a plausible cam type with a partial explanation.

Emerging (1): Names a cam profile with no explanation.

[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Galton Engineering produces bicycle brake assemblies. The brake lever is connected to the brake pads by a cable and a bell-crank linkage.

Evaluate whether using a bell-crank (reverse) linkage is the best mechanism for this application. In your answer, consider at least one alternative mechanism and compare them.
practice_questions.type: 8 marks — Extended Response: Evaluate an Engineering Decision
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8): Explains that a bell-crank linkage changes the direction of motion by 90°, allowing the cable tension from the hand lever (pulling along the handlebar) to be redirected to push brake pads perpendicular to the cable. Evaluates advantages (compact, reliable, no power loss, easily adjusted) and limitations (friction at pivot, requires correct alignment, cable stretch over time). Considers an alternative (direct pull cable, hydraulic disc brake) and compares it on relevant grounds (force, weight, cost, maintenance). Reaches a justified conclusion.

Secure (5-6): Explains the function of the bell-crank in changing motion direction, at least one advantage and one limitation, and some comparison with an alternative.

Developing (3-4): Partial explanation of the linkage function. Limited comparison with alternatives.

Emerging (1-2): Basic description of a linkage with minimal engineering reasoning.

[8 marks]

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of motion describes a pendulum swinging back and forth around a fixed pivot?
What determines the position of a follower at any point in a cam's rotation?
options: The radius of the cam at the point of contact
The length of the connecting rod

knowledge_checks.q: A crank and slider mechanism converts _____ motion into reciprocating linear motion.
A pear cam produces a slow rise followed by a quick _____ of the follower.
Match each cam profile to its motion characteristic:
right: Slow rise, quick drop — used in valve timing
Smooth, simple harmonic rise and fall
Gradual rise then sudden almost-vertical drop

flashcard_questions.a: Continuous circular movement around a fixed central axis.
Back-and-forth movement along a straight line, such as a piston.
Swinging or rocking about a fixed point, like a pendulum or windscreen wiper.
A mechanism of rigid bars connected by pivots that transmits or transforms motion and force.

flashcard_questions.q: What does a crank and slider mechanism do?
flashcard_questions.a: Converts rotary motion into reciprocating linear motion.
A shaped rotating disc that pushes a follower up and down as its profile changes.

flashcard_questions.q: What determines the position of a follower on a cam?
flashcard_questions.a: The radius of the cam at the point of contact with the follower.

flashcard_questions.q: Which cam profile produces a slow rise and a quick drop?
Which cam produces a smooth, simple harmonic rise and fall?
What motion does a windscreen wiper produce?
What is a bell-crank (reverse) linkage used for?
flashcard_questions.a: To change the direction of a force, typically by 90 degrees.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the type of motion produced by a car piston.

glossary_terms.definition: Continuous circular movement around a fixed central axis, such as a rotating shaft or wheel.
Movement in a straight line from one point to another.
Back-and-forth movement along a straight line, such as a piston in a cylinder.
Swinging or rocking movement about a central point, like a pendulum or a windscreen wiper.
A mechanism made of rigid bars (links) connected by pivots that transmits or transforms motion and force.
A mechanism that converts rotary motion into reciprocating linear motion, consisting of a rotating crank connected to a sliding element by a connecting rod.
A shaped plate or disc that rotates and pushes a follower up and down as its profile (outline) changes.
A component that rests against a cam and moves up and down as the cam rotates, following the cam's profile.
